core_obligations: D'Alembert splitting: introduce z+ = (1/2)(z0 - i A^{-1} z1), z- = (1/2)(z0 + i A^{-1} z1), inverting as z0 = z+ + z- and z1 = i A (z+ - z-); since (d/dt -+ iA) e^{+-itA} z+- = 0 one gets (d^2/dt^2 + A^2) e^{+-itA} z+- = 0 and the solution rewrites z(t) = e^{itA} z+ + e^{-itA} z- (lines 1833-1846).

Almost-isometry: for any s in R the splitting isomorphism Lambda : H_s x H_{s-2} -> H_s x H_s, Lambda(z0, z1) = (z+, z-), satisfies norm(z0,z1)^2_{H_s x H_{s-2}} = 2 (norm(z+)^2_{H_s} + norm(z-)^2_{H_s}); consequently the energy factorises E_s(z0, z1) = E_s(Lambda^{-1}(z+, z-)) (lines 1847-1859).

Cut-off observation identity: for T', T'' in (0,T) with T'' - T' > T~ and rho in C_c^infty equal to 1 on (T',T'') with support in (0,T), the observed square splits into the two decoupled terms plus/minus twice the real part of the interaction term int rho^2 < C A e^{itA} z+, C A e^{-itA} z- >_Y, with opposite signs for C and C1 (lines 1861-1877).

Decoupled lower bound: by commutativity of A with e^{+-i . A} the weak observability of the first-order system (4.3) gives int_0^T norm(rho C A e^{+-itA} z+-)^2_Y dt >= (1/C)(norm(A z+-)^2_{H_0} - norm(A z+-)^2_{H_{-2}}), and adding both signs yields (1/2C)(E_2(Lambda^{-1}(z0,z1)) - E_0(Lambda^{-1}(z0,z1))) = (1/2C)(E_2(z0,z1) - E_0(z0,z1)) (lines 1878-1888).

Interaction term estimate by spectral expansion: with Fourier coefficients z_{+-,k} = < z+-, e_k >_{H_0} the interaction term is sum_{j,k} z_{+,j} z_{-,k} < C A e_j, C A e_k >_Y times the oscillatory integral of rho^2; boundedness of C : H_2 -> Y gives |< C e_j, C e_k >_Y| <= C lambda_j lambda_k, the Fourier decay |hat{rho^2}(xi)| <= C_N <xi>^{-N} bounds the oscillatory integral by C_N (lambda_j lambda_k)^{-N/2}, and choosing N large enough that sum_j lambda_j^{1-N/2} converges by the Weyl-type hypothesis (4.2) the whole interaction term is absorbed by 2 norm(z0,z1)^2_{H_0 x H_{-2}}, concluding both weak observability inequalities (lines 1889-1897).
proof_roadmap: Split the Cauchy data into the e^{itA} and e^{-itA} components and identify the splitting isomorphism.
Record the almost-isometry property of the splitting.
Write the cut-off observation identity separating decoupled and interaction terms.
Bound the decoupled terms with the weak observability of the first-order system.
Absorb the interaction term through its spectral expansion, operator boundedness and Fourier decay, choosing the exponent N via the Weyl-type hypothesis.
historical_task.difficulty_reason: Long functional-analytic proof combining a d'Alembert factorisation, energy bookkeeping across scales, and a spectral absorption argument whose convergence exponent must be tuned against the Weyl-type hypothesis.

historical_task.title: Unique continuation for the plate-like equation under weak observability

statement_spans.label: author proposition environment, source label prop:nt-plates (statement, source lines 1905-1912)

proof_spans.label: the author's own proof environment immediately following it (source lines 1913-1952)

core_obligations: Kernel and basic estimate: for the observation by C, the null set N_T = {(z0,z1) in H_2 x H_0 : C e^{tA}(z0,z1) = 0 in L^2([0,T],Y)} is a linear subspace by linearity of the equation, and the weak observability of Proposition 4.6 restricted to N_T gives the inequality norm(z0,z1)_{H_2 x H_0} <= C norm(z0,z1)_{H_0 x H_{-2}} (labelled prop:ineq:plates_nt, inside the proof span) (lines 1914-1923).

Semigroup smoothing: for 0 < eps < T - T~ and (z0,z1) in N_T the difference quotients (z0^eps, z1^eps) = (1/eps)(e^{eps A}(z0,z1) - (z0,z1)) belong to N_{T~}; since (A^{-1}z0, A^{-1}z1) in D(A), classical semigroup theory gives (A^{-1}z0^eps, A^{-1}z1^eps) -> A(A^{-1}z0, A^{-1}z1) = (z0,z1) in H_2 x H_0; the family is Cauchy for norm_{H_0 x H_{-2}} and, by the basic estimate, for norm_{H_2 x H_0}, so the limit lies in H_2 x H_0 and N_T is contained in D(A) (lines 1925-1935).

Invariance under the generator: the time regularity of e^{tA} permits differentiating the observation condition, partial_t C e^{tA}(z0,z1) = C e^{tA} A(z0,z1), so N_T is stable under A and contains only elements of D(A^k) x D(A^k) for every k (lines 1936-1938).

Finite dimensionality: applying the basic estimate to A(z0,z1) yields norm(z0,z1)_{H_4 x H_2} <= C norm(z0,z1)_{H_2 x H_0}; the unit ball of N_T in the H_2 x H_0 topology is bounded in H_4 x H_2, hence compact by the compact embedding (A has compact resolvent), and by Riesz's theorem N_T is finite-dimensional (lines 1940-1942).

Contradiction through the eigenvalue problem: -A^2 is self-adjoint positive and preserves N_T, so it has an eigenvalue lambda >= 0 with eigenvector (v_lambda, w_lambda) satisfying A^2 v_lambda = lambda v_lambda, A^2 w_lambda = lambda w_lambda; writing lambda = alpha^2 with alpha > 0 (A^2 strictly positive) gives (A + alpha I)(A - alpha I) v_lambda = 0, whence A v_lambda = alpha v_lambda and A w_lambda = alpha w_lambda; the explicit group law for e^{tA}(v_lambda, w_lambda) and the observation condition force C A v_lambda = C A w_lambda = 0 on [0,T], and Assumption UCP with alpha != 0 gives (v_lambda, w_lambda) = (0,0), contradicting N_T != {0} (lines 1943-1950).

Observation by C1: the same argument leads to the unique continuation problem -alpha sin(alpha t) C v_lambda + alpha cos(alpha t) C w_lambda = 0 for t in [0,T], to which Assumption UCP still applies (lines 1951-1952).
proof_roadmap: Define the null space of the observation and transfer the weak observability estimate to it.
Smooth the null data with semigroup difference quotients and conclude N_T lies in the generator's domain.
Show invariance of the null space under the generator and infinite-order regularity of its elements.
Derive finite dimensionality from the compact embedding and Riesz's theorem.
Build the eigenvalue contradiction from the self-adjoint operator -A^2 and the unique continuation assumption, for both observation operators.
historical_task.difficulty_reason: Compactness-plus-unique-continuation argument: several functional-analytic steps (semigroup smoothing, Riesz finite dimensionality, explicit group law on the eigenvector) must be assembled in the right order.

historical_task.title: Existence, uniqueness and estimate for the observability Cauchy problem

statement_spans.label: author lemma environment, source label lmCauchyobs (statement, source lines 513-527)

proof_spans.label: the author's own proof environment immediately following it (source lines 528-578)

core_obligations: Duhamel reduction: being a solution of the first line of the projected system is equivalent to W(t) = e^{tA} W0 + I(t) Q_n H for some W0 in Q_n X^sigma (W lies in C^0([0,T], Q_n X^sigma) subset L^2), so only W0 must be computed (lines 529-532).

Observability projection identity: for W0 in Q_n X^sigma one has C[e^{.A} W0] = O W0 = O_n W0, hence Pi_n C[e^{.A} W0] = O_n W0; imposing Pi_n C W = Pi_n G and inverting gives W0 = O_n^{-1} Pi_n [G - C I(.) Q_n H], and reproducing the computation backward verifies the second line of the projected system (lines 533-547).

Uniqueness: for two solutions the difference R = W1 - W2 satisfies the homogeneous system d/dt R = A R, Pi_n C R = 0, so R(t) = e^{tA} R(0) and Pi_n C R = Pi_n O R(0) = O_n R(0); injectivity of O_n forces R(0) = 0 (lines 548-555).

Semigroup and observability bounds: skew-adjointness of A on X^sigma gives the standard estimate norm(W)_{C^0} <= norm(W0)_{X^sigma} + norm(Q_n H)_{L^1}; applying the observability bound (2.5) to Pi_n G-tilde in Y_n gives norm(O_n^{-1} Pi_n G-tilde)_{X^sigma} <= C_obs norm(Pi_n G-tilde)_{L^2}, hence W0 is bounded by C_obs (norm(Pi_n G)_{L^2} + norm(Pi_n C I(.) Q_n H)_{L^2}) (lines 557-568).

Time Holder + unitarity conclusion: unitarity of Pi_n and the norm bound for C give norm(C I(.) Q_n H)_{L^2} <= T^{1/2} norm(C)_{L(X^sigma)} norm(Q_n H)_{L^1}; combining with the W0 bound and the semigroup estimate yields the final estimate for F_n(G,H) in C^0([0,T], Q_n X^sigma) (lines 569-577).
proof_roadmap: Rewrite the projected Cauchy problem as a Duhamel formula and reduce everything to computing W0.
Use the identity C e^{.A} = O on Q_n X^sigma to solve the projection constraint for W0 explicitly.
Prove uniqueness through the homogeneous difference system and injectivity of O_n.
Bound W by the semigroup estimate, bound W0 through the observability inequality (2.5), and absorb the I(.) Q_n H term by Holder in time and unitarity of Pi_n.
historical_task.difficulty_reason: Multi-part functional-analytic well-posedness proof for a finite-rank projected Cauchy problem: Duhamel bookkeeping, a projection identity, an injectivity argument and a chain of semigroup/observability estimates that must be recombined into one constant.

statement_spans.label: author proposition environment, source label prop:nt-plates (statement, source lines 1905-1912)

proof_spans.label: the author's own proof environment immediately following it (source lines 1913-1952)

core_obligations: Kernel and basic estimate: for the observation by C, the null set N_T = {(z0,z1) in H_2 x H_0 : C e^{tA}(z0,z1) = 0 in L^2([0,T],Y)} is a linear subspace by linearity of the equation, and the weak observability of Proposition 4.6 restricted to N_T gives the inequality norm(z0,z1)_{H_2 x H_0} <= C norm(z0,z1)_{H_0 x H_{-2}} (labelled prop:ineq:plates_nt, inside the proof span) (lines 1914-1923).

Semigroup smoothing: for 0 < eps < T - T~ and (z0,z1) in N_T the difference quotients (z0^eps, z1^eps) = (1/eps)(e^{eps A}(z0,z1) - (z0,z1)) belong to N_{T~}; since (A^{-1}z0, A^{-1}z1) in D(A), classical semigroup theory gives (A^{-1}z0^eps, A^{-1}z1^eps) -> A(A^{-1}z0, A^{-1}z1) = (z0,z1) in H_2 x H_0; the family is Cauchy for norm_{H_0 x H_{-2}} and, by the basic estimate, for norm_{H_2 x H_0}, so the limit lies in H_2 x H_0 and N_T is contained in D(A) (lines 1925-1935).

Invariance under the generator: the time regularity of e^{tA} permits differentiating the observation condition, partial_t C e^{tA}(z0,z1) = C e^{tA} A(z0,z1), so N_T is stable under A and contains only elements of D(A^k) x D(A^k) for every k (lines 1936-1938).

Finite dimensionality: applying the basic estimate to A(z0,z1) yields norm(z0,z1)_{H_4 x H_2} <= C norm(z0,z1)_{H_2 x H_0}; the unit ball of N_T in the H_2 x H_0 topology is bounded in H_4 x H_2, hence compact by the compact embedding (A has compact resolvent), and by Riesz's theorem N_T is finite-dimensional (lines 1940-1942).

Contradiction through the eigenvalue problem: -A^2 is self-adjoint positive and preserves N_T, so it has an eigenvalue lambda >= 0 with eigenvector (v_lambda, w_lambda) satisfying A^2 v_lambda = lambda v_lambda, A^2 w_lambda = lambda w_lambda; writing lambda = alpha^2 with alpha > 0 (A^2 strictly positive) gives (A + alpha I)(A - alpha I) v_lambda = 0, whence A v_lambda = alpha v_lambda and A w_lambda = alpha w_lambda; the explicit group law for e^{tA}(v_lambda, w_lambda) and the observation condition force C A v_lambda = C A w_lambda = 0 on [0,T], and Assumption UCP with alpha != 0 gives (v_lambda, w_lambda) = (0,0), contradicting N_T != {0} (lines 1943-1950).

Observation by C1: the same argument leads to the unique continuation problem -alpha sin(alpha t) C v_lambda + alpha cos(alpha t) C w_lambda = 0 for t in [0,T], to which Assumption UCP still applies (lines 1951-1952).
proof_roadmap: Define the null space of the observation and transfer the weak observability estimate to it.
Smooth the null data with semigroup difference quotients and conclude N_T lies in the generator's domain.
Show invariance of the null space under the generator and infinite-order regularity of its elements.
Derive finite dimensionality from the compact embedding and Riesz's theorem.
Build the eigenvalue contradiction from the self-adjoint operator -A^2 and the unique continuation assumption, for both observation operators.
historical_task.difficulty_reason: Compactness-plus-unique-continuation argument: several functional-analytic steps (semigroup smoothing, Riesz finite dimensionality, explicit group law on the eigenvector) must be assembled in the right order.

proof_spans.label: the author's own proof environment immediately following it (source lines 1832-1897)

core_obligations: D'Alembert splitting: introduce z+ = (1/2)(z0 - i A^{-1} z1), z- = (1/2)(z0 + i A^{-1} z1), inverting as z0 = z+ + z- and z1 = i A (z+ - z-); since (d/dt -+ iA) e^{+-itA} z+- = 0 one gets (d^2/dt^2 + A^2) e^{+-itA} z+- = 0 and the solution rewrites z(t) = e^{itA} z+ + e^{-itA} z- (lines 1833-1846).

Almost-isometry: for any s in R the splitting isomorphism Lambda : H_s x H_{s-2} -> H_s x H_s, Lambda(z0, z1) = (z+, z-), satisfies norm(z0,z1)^2_{H_s x H_{s-2}} = 2 (norm(z+)^2_{H_s} + norm(z-)^2_{H_s}); consequently the energy factorises E_s(z0, z1) = E_s(Lambda^{-1}(z+, z-)) (lines 1847-1859).

Cut-off observation identity: for T', T'' in (0,T) with T'' - T' > T~ and rho in C_c^infty equal to 1 on (T',T'') with support in (0,T), the observed square splits into the two decoupled terms plus/minus twice the real part of the interaction term int rho^2 < C A e^{itA} z+, C A e^{-itA} z- >_Y, with opposite signs for C and C1 (lines 1861-1877).

Decoupled lower bound: by commutativity of A with e^{+-i . A} the weak observability of the first-order system (4.3) gives int_0^T norm(rho C A e^{+-itA} z+-)^2_Y dt >= (1/C)(norm(A z+-)^2_{H_0} - norm(A z+-)^2_{H_{-2}}), and adding both signs yields (1/2C)(E_2(Lambda^{-1}(z0,z1)) - E_0(Lambda^{-1}(z0,z1))) = (1/2C)(E_2(z0,z1) - E_0(z0,z1)) (lines 1878-1888).

Interaction term estimate by spectral expansion: with Fourier coefficients z_{+-,k} = < z+-, e_k >_{H_0} the interaction term is sum_{j,k} z_{+,j} z_{-,k} < C A e_j, C A e_k >_Y times the oscillatory integral of rho^2; boundedness of C : H_2 -> Y gives |< C e_j, C e_k >_Y| <= C lambda_j lambda_k, the Fourier decay |hat{rho^2}(xi)| <= C_N <xi>^{-N} bounds the oscillatory integral by C_N (lambda_j lambda_k)^{-N/2}, and choosing N large enough that sum_j lambda_j^{1-N/2} converges by the Weyl-type hypothesis (4.2) the whole interaction term is absorbed by 2 norm(z0,z1)^2_{H_0 x H_{-2}}, concluding both weak observability inequalities (lines 1889-1897).
proof_roadmap: Split the Cauchy data into the e^{itA} and e^{-itA} components and identify the splitting isomorphism.
Record the almost-isometry property of the splitting.
Write the cut-off observation identity separating decoupled and interaction terms.
Bound the decoupled terms with the weak observability of the first-order system.
Absorb the interaction term through its spectral expansion, operator boundedness and Fourier decay, choosing the exponent N via the Weyl-type hypothesis.
historical_task.difficulty_reason: Long functional-analytic proof combining a d'Alembert factorisation, energy bookkeeping across scales, and a spectral absorption argument whose convergence exponent must be tuned against the Weyl-type hypothesis.
